title: Indian Americans Keep Six House Seats as Ramaswamy Loses Ohio Governor Race
excerpt: Four returning Democrats — Bera, Khanna, Jayapal and Subramanyam — will be joined by newcomers Pia Dandiya of Florida and Amish Shah of Arizona, while Vivek Ramaswamy's Trump-backed bid for Ohio governor fell short.
body:
• Indian Americans will hold six seats in the US House in the new Congress — four returning Democrats and two newcomers, Pia Dandiya in Florida and Amish Shah in Arizona.
  • Every Indian American who won a House race is a Democrat, and the full group will sit in the House majority when the new Congress convenes in January.
  • The biggest loss: Vivek Ramaswamy, endorsed by President Trump, lost the Ohio governor's race to Democrat Amy Acton.
  • Down the ballot, a post-election tally counted 30 Indian-American wins in state legislative races, and Nithya Raman won the Los Angeles mayor's race.

Indian-American candidates ended the November 3 midterms holding their ground on Capitol Hill and gaining ground almost everywhere else. Six Indian Americans were elected to the US House of Representatives, matching the community's record, while the night's most prominent Indian-American candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy, lost his bid for Ohio governor.

The six in the House

The returning members are Ami Bera of California, the longest-serving Indian American in Congress, first elected in 2012; Ro Khanna of California's Silicon Valley district, who defeated fellow Indian American Ritesh Tandon, a Republican; Pramila Jayapal of Washington, the first South Asian-American woman elected to Congress, in 2016; and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia, who secured a second term, The Indian Panorama reported in its post-election tally.

"https://www.instagram.com/reel/DfH6Vd-ukc2/ The two newcomers replace the representation lost when Raja Krishnamoorthi and Shri Thanedar were defeated in earlier primary contests."

The two newcomers replace the representation lost when Raja Krishnamoorthi and Shri Thanedar were defeated in earlier primary contests. Pia Dandiya, a former teacher and high school principal, defeated Republican Casey Askar in Florida's 22nd District, becoming the first Indian-American woman elected to the House from Florida; she won with roughly 52 percent of the vote. Amish Shah, a physician and former Arizona state legislator, defeated Republican Jay Feely in Arizona's 1st District, becoming the first Indian American elected to Congress from Arizona. Every Indian American House winner is a Democrat, so the entire group will be part of the majority starting in January.

The losses

Ramaswamy's defeat was the night's headline loss. The Republican, backed by President Trump, lost the Ohio gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Acton, despite outspending her five to one, according to Firstpost America's election coverage. In New York, Republican Saritha Komatireddy lost the attorney general's race to incumbent Democrat Letitia James. The other Indian-American Republican and independent federal candidates also lost, including Tandon in California, Nirav Sheth in Washington and Mahesh Ganorkar in North Carolina.

Beyond Washington

In Maryland, Indian-born Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller won another term alongside Democratic Governor Wes Moore. A post-election tally published by India Tribune counted 30 Indian-American winners in state legislative races, including eight who faced no opposition; The Indian Panorama notes those state figures remain subject to final reconciliation with official results. Among the firsts: Jyot Singh became the first Indian American and first Sikh American elected to Georgia's General Assembly, and Pooja Sethi became the first Indian-American woman elected to the Texas Legislature.

The largest municipal prize went to Nithya Raman, born in Kerala, who defeated incumbent Karen Bass to become mayor of Los Angeles. For a community long identified with medicine, technology and business, the 2026 map now runs from six House seats to a big-city mayor's office — and, after these results, entirely through one party at the federal level.
